source: AI-assisted content generation (ChatGPT), general veterinary disease-recognition best practice (ASF, CSF, FMD, swine dysentery) — pending farmer/RUA verification
text: For smallholder pig farmers in Preah Vihear, recognizing disease means noticing changes from normal behavior rather than diagnosing from one symptom. Important diseases include African swine fever (ASF — high fever, depression, loss of appetite, weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, skin redness/hemorrhages, abortion, sudden death; can have extremely high mortality), classical swine fever (CSF — fever, huddling, weakness, conjunctivitis, digestive disturbance, unsteady movement, purplish skin discoloration), foot-and-mouth disease (fever, salivation, mouth/foot lesions, severe lameness), and swine dysentery (progressively severe diarrhea with mucus/blood, dehydration, weight loss). ASF and CSF can look very similar and symptoms alone cannot reliably distinguish them — the chatbot should never tell a farmer a pig definitely has ASF or CSF from symptoms alone. During the wet season (roughly May–October), watch for muddy housing, standing water, contaminated equipment, and increased animal contact; during the dry season (roughly November–April), heat stress, dehydration, and dust increase concern. These conditions can worsen problems but do not by themselves identify a disease. Sudden unexplained deaths, rapidly spreading illness, high fever with hemorrhagic signs, severe bloody diarrhea, or multiple sick animals should trigger urgent action: minimize animal movement/sales, separate affected animals where feasible, avoid moving potentially contaminated equipment between pens, and contact a veterinarian or animal-health authority. No treatment or vaccine doses should be given as universal facts. No specific pig breed is assigned as predominant in Preah Vihear without reliable evidence.
